lxc_8ad12ffb1d3aa87f.text: Some villains are easy to hate and hard to ignore.

lxc_15f4ff722f26df37.text: Stories can use the mind's attention to danger, curiosity about missing information, safe excitement, and uncertainty about motives.

lxc_eca0b2e6927f72f3.text: Four research studies help explain why a bad character can be an excellent engine for a story.

lxc_15fbb98a749c87a1.text: K. Maja Krakowiak and Mary Beth Oliver compared stories with good, bad, or morally mixed characters.

lxc_7f74fd4337c8a73b.text: The bad characters were liked the least.

lxc_9447222edfe6c319.text: However, their stories were just as suspenseful and mentally engaging as the others.

lxc_8bdc1758e242456a.text: This gives us the first answer: liking a character and paying attention to a character are different.

lxc_9c788c6ae4331f06.text: A villain can be unpleasant and still make a story difficult to leave.

lxc_5a9ef15096d5011c.text: Psychologist Arne Öhman and his team asked people to find one different face in a grid.

lxc_f349611dd52cbb32.text: Across five experiments, people found threatening faces faster and more accurately than friendly faces.

lxc_d0e11f8aecad3fcb.text: This was not a study of villains, so it is only one part of the answer.

lxc_9c1c9aeb004db274.text: It shows a useful part of attention: possible danger can get priority.

lxc_75a06e80f5d04e31.text: A fictional villain adds plans and choices, so we keep watching for what that person might do next.

lxc_9601d1d6c2413e8c.text: Psychologist Coltan Scrivner developed a 24-question Morbid Curiosity Scale.

lxc_c30ae594af51209a.text: It measures interest in four areas: dangerous minds, violence between people, injured bodies, and paranormal danger.

lxc_cbbf752fc4b5a98b.text: In the final experiment, people chose between dark and neutral pictures or descriptions.

lxc_b0fce8845047eb4f.text: People with higher scores were more likely to choose the dark information.

lxc_159504c84bdf5fa0.text: Villains fit one area especially well: the minds of dangerous people.

lxc_dcf7e40899f90c8a.text: We want to know the motive, plan, or hidden history.

lxc_c7bf94113d709407.text: Paul Rozin and his team studied 29 experiences that usually feel unpleasant, including fear, sadness, pain, strong tastes, and physical exhaustion.

lxc_0ae5b0ea2717aae7.text: Many people said they enjoyed some of them when the experience was safe.

lxc_cce71989c34b9a12.text: The researchers called this benign masochism.

lxc_31df15de1debbfac.text: A frightening story can work in a similar way.

lxc_2cd04e8a79b4fc3d.text: Your body reacts, but your mind knows you can pause the film or close the book.

lxc_92606fd2a46353e5.text: The danger feels real enough to be exciting, but not real enough to hurt you.

lxc_c11dbb67b96d647c.text: Some villains are not simply cruel.

lxc_069258c56f62c88d.text: They may love one person, protect a group, or regret one choice while continuing to cause harm.

lxc_9e47569793810c9b.text: This creates moral ambiguity: we can understand part of the character without approving of the action.

lxc_b70bf0396b0991aa.text: In Krakowiak and Oliver's study, morally mixed characters were liked less than good characters, yet their stories were equally suspenseful, engaging, and enjoyable.

lxc_2de65e2ea5a95a90.text: When several motives are possible, the audience keeps testing predictions: Will the villain change, repeat the harm, or surprise us?

lxc_57b02124281efa5b.text: Darth Vader brings threat, but his past also creates a question about change.

lxc_5fa6581ee36601df.text: Iago in Othello tells the audience about his plan, so suspense comes from waiting to see who will understand the trap.

lxc_98490ad745f8de88.text: Frankenstein's creature causes harm but also describes rejection and loneliness, which creates moral ambiguity.

lxc_ae0eac40f8543072.text: Fun fact: Mary Shelley never gives the creature a personal name; Frankenstein is the creator.
